entries.clue: That’s all on Feds busting politician (3,2,5)

indicatorNotes.busting: A bust breaks the place apart, and the two words beside it come apart into loose letters rather than staying as printed.

blocks.note: six letters shaken out of those two words
a Tory is a British Conservative, the politician crosswords reach for first

annotation.surface: Federal agents arresting a politician, and nothing more to be said about him.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' reads as a link word and is fodder instead, which is why the anagram looks two letters too short. The Feds bust people; here they bust letters.
annotation.definitionFit: That’s all → END OF STORY: both are what you say to shut a subject down, with nothing further coming.

entries.clue: Food waste at several stores (4)

indicatorNotes.stores: A store keeps things inside it, so what is wanted is already sitting within the words rather than being made out of them.

blocks.note: four letters in a row, beginning on the last letter of the first word

annotation.surface: Several shops throwing out food that has gone off.
annotation.walkthrough: The run straddles two word-breaks, which is what keeps it out of sight. Eats as a noun survives in invitations promising good eats.
annotation.definitionFit: Food → EATS: eats is the plural noun for things to eat, exactly what is laid on at a party.

entries.clue: Flat flatfish: that’s about right (4)

indicatorNotes.about: To be about a thing is to be all round it, so the word named before closes over the letter named after.

blocks.note: the dab is a small flatfish landed off British coasts
R is the standard short form of right, as on a map or a stage direction

annotation.surface: Agreeing that a flatfish is indeed flat.
annotation.walkthrough: Flat is doing the dull job here, not the level one: a flat afternoon, a flat performance. The dab is the crossword's usual flatfish.
annotation.definitionFit: Flat → DRAB: a flat colour or a flat voice has no life in it, which is what drab says of anything dreary.

entries.clue: Delicate creatures tomorrow and for another week, according to one’s horoscope? (12)

blocks.note: the puzzle ran on a Thursday, so tomorrow was Friday, FRI in any diary
the span does not stop at Friday but runs on, and a run-on date is written Fri till whatever ends it
Aries opens around 21 March, about a week past that Friday

annotation.surface: A horoscope covering tomorrow and the week that follows it.
annotation.walkthrough: Fritillaries are both chequered orange butterflies and drooping snake's-head flowers, and 'creatures' picks the insect. The dates only work for a puzzle printed in mid-March.
annotation.definitionFit: Delicate creatures → FRITILLARIES: the fritillary butterflies are thin-winged and short-lived, and 'creatures' settles that the animal is meant, not the flower.

blocks.note: 17 is THUMB and 21 is THING, so this reads as 'something to sing', and the lisp that made 'thumb thing' out of 'something' turns the S of the answer into TH

annotation.walkthrough: Both halves have to be read with a lisp: 17 and 21 together say 'something', and 21 on its own says 'sing'. Nothing in the clue says so — the cross-references do it.
annotation.definitionFit: 17 21 brief → THONG: unlisped that is 'something brief', and a thong is the briefest underwear made, briefs being the word for pants anyway.

entries.clue: People staying at home, and stumbling, hopeful steps taken before a fall? (4,5)

annotation.definition: hopeful steps taken before a fall?

indicatorNotes.staying: To stay somewhere is to lodge inside it, so what follows takes up residence within the letters named before.
indicatorNotes.stumbling: A stumble puts a foot down in the wrong place, and the word beside it lands its letters in the wrong places too.

blocks.note: a people is a race — the Basque people, the Basque race
someone at home is in, the way a caller is told the lady of the house is in
the three letters of the little word itself, resettled

annotation.surface: People shut up indoors, tripping about in a hopeful shuffle.
annotation.walkthrough: The fall being hoped for is rainfall, not a tumble, though 'stumbling' works hard to keep you thinking of the tumble.
annotation.definitionFit: hopeful steps taken before a fall? → RAIN DANCE: the dance is meant to bring rain down, so the steps come first and the downpour follows.

entries.clue: Swinging both ways in the guise of intolerance (4)

blocks.note: someone who swings both ways is bi, short for bisexual
to turn up in the guise of a thing is to turn up as it

annotation.surface: Someone who swings both ways posing as a bigot.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In the guise of' looks like a disguise instruction and is simply the word 'as' spelt out. A leaning to one side is the opposite of the surface's swinging both ways.
annotation.definitionFit: intolerance → BIAS: a bias is a settled leaning against one side, which is what intolerance of that side comes down to.

entries.clue: Short, and a quite misshapen nose, ultimately (10)

indicatorNotes.misshapen: What is misshapen has been pushed out of its proper shape, and the letters named take on a new shape too.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately points at the very end, so only the final letter of the word before it is wanted.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder, taken straight off the page
the last letter of the word

annotation.surface: A nose that has ended up rather badly out of shape.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short' is not about length but about falling short, coming up under what was needed. The comma after it is the only sign it stands apart.
annotation.definitionFit: Short → INADEQUATE: supplies that are short do not stretch to what is wanted, which is what inadequate says of them.

entries.clue: Unctuous windbag, potential killer? (6-4)

blocks.note: an unctuous manner is an oily, smooth one
a windbag talks on and on, which makes him a bore

annotation.surface: An oily, droning man who might turn out to be dangerous.
annotation.walkthrough: A smooth-bore is a gun barrel left unrifled inside — muskets and shotguns are smooth-bores — so two insults about a man stack up into a weapon.
annotation.definitionFit: potential killer? → SMOOTH-BORE: the answer is an unrifled gun barrel, named here by what it might do rather than by what it is.

entries.clue: Seriously funny minute where head blown off in which Groucho’s prop backfires? (10)

indicatorNotes.blown off: What is blown off is gone, so the letter named beside it never reaches the answer.
indicatorNotes.in which: In which names the word the next piece is to be dropped inside.
indicatorNotes.backfires: A backfire goes off the wrong way round, and the letters named come out back to front.

blocks.note: minute means atomic, small as an atom, not the unit of time
the head of that word is its opening letter, and it is the A that goes
Groucho Marx was never photographed without a cigar, and those five letters arrive the other way round

annotation.surface: A gag in which the cigar goes off in Groucho Marx's face.
annotation.walkthrough: Tragicomedy is the stage genre that plays grief for laughs, so the definition is not the contradiction it looks. 'Minute' is the adjective, said mi-NEWT.
annotation.definitionFit: Seriously funny → TRAGICOMIC: a tragicomic tale is grave and funny at the same moment, and the word splits into exactly those two halves.

entries.clue: Equerry’s rump plastered in red sauce (4)

indicatorNotes.rump: The rump is the hind end, so only the final letter of the word before it is taken.
indicatorNotes.plastered in: Plastered into something is spread right inside it, so that letter lands within the word that follows.

blocks.note: Chairman Mao led communist China, and a communist is a red
the hind end of the word is its Y

annotation.surface: Red sauce smeared across a royal attendant's backside.
annotation.walkthrough: An equerry is an officer who attends a member of the royal family. Nothing about the answer is red — that colour belongs to the Chairman.
annotation.definitionFit: sauce → MAYO: mayo is the everyday short form of mayonnaise, the sauce squeezed over chips and sandwiches.

entries.clue: Show agony and sign the forms (8,4)

indicatorNotes.forms: What forms takes on a shape it did not have, so the letters settle into an arrangement they did not start in.

blocks.note: five letters of fodder
seven more, straight off the page

annotation.surface: Wincing through a pile of paperwork and signing it anyway.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Show agony' reads as verb and object, which is how a one-word definition hides at the front. Cole Porter's 1934 musical is the show meant.
annotation.definitionFit: Show → ANYTHING GOES: Cole Porter's musical, revived often enough that 'show' names it the way it names any long-running musical.

entries.clue: Fly, say, in starter of soup etc, dining we found funny? (6,6)

indicatorNotes.starter of: The starter is the first course, so only the first letter of the word after it is served up.
indicatorNotes.found funny: Something found funny strikes people as odd, and letters in an odd order are letters that have been moved.

blocks.note: the opening letter of the word
eleven more letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Finding something funny about a fly in the first course of a meal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the giveaway that the definition is by example: a fly is one of thousands that qualify. The comma after 'etc' hides the join in the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: Fly, say → WINGED INSECT: the housefly is one instance of the group, and 'say' signals that the wider class is wanted.

entries.clue: Heart palpitating over wife in bedroom, tickler of infant’s bottom? (10)

indicatorNotes.palpitating: A palpitating heart thumps unevenly, and the word beside it gives up its letters unevenly too.
indicatorNotes.over: In a down clue over is a position, not a turn: what it follows sits higher up the column than the rest.
indicatorNotes.in: In drops what is named before it inside the word named after it.

blocks.note: the five letters of the word, shaken up
a dorm is a room full of beds in a school or a hostel
w is the standard short form of wife, as on a family tree

annotation.surface: A racing heart over a wife in the bedroom.
annotation.walkthrough: Threadworms are the pinworms small children pick up at school, and the itch they set off is the 'tickler'. The surface keeps the word bottom for the joke.
annotation.definitionFit: tickler of infant’s bottom? → THREADWORM: the worm lays its eggs around a child's anus, and the itching that follows is the whole of its bad reputation.

entries.clue: Back stabbed by company in African country – warmer in Asia? (6,4)

indicatorNotes.stabbed by: A stab goes into the body, so whatever does the stabbing finishes up inside the word named before.
indicatorNotes.in: In puts what comes before it within what comes after.

blocks.note: aft is the back end of a ship
Ghana is on the west coast of Africa
Co is the short form on any letterhead — Smith & Co

annotation.surface: Someone knifed by a firm out in an African country.
annotation.walkthrough: The insertion runs two deep: the firm goes into the country, and country and firm together go into the ship's back end. An Afghan coat is the shaggy sheepskin the 1960s made famous.
annotation.definitionFit: warmer in Asia? → AFGHAN COAT: the coat takes its name from Afghanistan, and a lined sheepskin is about the warmest thing anyone wears.

entries.clue: Pompous, more than is usual at an airport, did you say? (9)

indicatorNotes.did you say?: Did you say asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling.

blocks.clueFragment: more than is usual at an airport
blocks.note: Luton is a London airport thirty miles north of the city, and an aircraft above the normal approach there is high for Luton

annotation.surface: An aircraft climbing higher than it normally would over an airport.
annotation.walkthrough: Said quickly, the airport disappears into the word. The usual spelling is high-falutin, American slang for airs and graces, and Paul takes the shorter form.
annotation.definitionFit: Pompous → HIFALUTIN: hifalutin talk is grand, self-important talk from someone giving themselves airs.

entries.clue: A packet with something sticky, work on sweetie that’s wrapped up (3,6)

indicatorNotes.on: In a down clue on means sitting on top, so the piece named first lies above the piece named after it.
indicatorNotes.that’s wrapped up: Wrapped up has paper closed round it, so the first letters named close over everything else.

blocks.note: tar is the black sticky stuff laid on roads
op is short for opus, the number a composer puts on a work
calling someone doll is the same endearment as calling them sweetie

annotation.surface: A parcel of something sticky and a present for a sweetheart, all gift-wrapped.
annotation.walkthrough: 'A packet' is money: to make a packet is to make a fortune, and to pay top dollar is to pay the very most asked. The definition is the first two words, before the wrapping starts.
annotation.definitionFit: A packet → TOP DOLLAR: both name a sum at the high end, and paying top dollar for a thing is paying a packet for it.

entries.clue: Hitch where consumption disturbed by whiff (5)

indicatorNotes.disturbed by: To be disturbed by something is to have it break in on you, so those letters land inside.

blocks.note: TB is tuberculosis, the disease once called consumption
a hum is a bad smell in British usage — a bin that hums gives off a whiff

annotation.surface: A coughing patient put off by a bad smell.
annotation.walkthrough: To thumb a lift and to hitch one are the same roadside gesture, which is where the definition comes from. 'Consumption' points at eating and means the illness.
annotation.definitionFit: Hitch → THUMB: to thumb a lift is to hitch one, sticking a thumb out at passing traffic.

entries.clue: III wrong? Alternatively, I or II divided by the number (5)

indicatorNotes.divided by: What is divided has been split down the middle, and whatever does the dividing sits in the gap.

blocks.note: ER is the royal cipher, Elizabeth Regina, and Britain has had an Elizabeth I and an Elizabeth II
the little word itself, dropped into the gap
a whole second route to the same five letters — III is THREE, and its letters come out wrong — with 'alternatively' handing over to the reading above

annotation.surface: Checking Roman numerals: if three is wrong, then it is one or two.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The number' is not a figure but a numb-er, the thing that numbs: ether was the anaesthetic of the Victorian operating theatre. Paul lays down two routes to the letters and either one gets there.
annotation.definitionFit: number → ETHER: ether numbs a patient, so the one that numbs is the number — the word read as numb-er rather than as a figure.

entries.clue: Colour in image on rock for sign (9)

indicatorNotes.in: In drops the letters named before it inside the word named after.
indicatorNotes.on: A picture painted on a rock lies over the rock's face, so the image is named first and the rock's letters follow.

blocks.note: pic is the everyday short form of picture
red is the colour crosswords reach for first
a tor is a rocky outcrop crowning a hill, as on Dartmoor

annotation.surface: Colouring in an image painted on a rock.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Colour in' looks like one instruction out of a child's book and is two: a colour, then the word that puts it inside. Rock art is ancient enough to make the surface sit still.
annotation.definitionFit: sign → PREDICTOR: a sign of what is coming is a predictor — the falling barometer that tells you rain is on the way.

entries.clue: Some Sandinista, get role in a dictatorship after revolution – would I? (6,6)

annotation.definition: Some Sandinista, get role in a dictatorship after revolution – would I?

indicatorNotes.Some: Some of the words means a part of them, so the letters wanted are already sitting in the clue in an unbroken row.
indicatorNotes.after revolution: A revolution turns a thing right round, so that row of letters is read from its far end backwards.

blocks.clueFragment: Sandinista, get role in a dictatorship
blocks.note: twelve letters in a row, from the last letter of the first word to the first letter of the last

annotation.surface: A revolutionary asking whether he would ever take a job under a dictatorship.
annotation.walkthrough: The run starts on the final A of Sandinista, which is why the hiding place is so hard to see. The Sandinistas were the guerrillas who overthrew Nicaragua's Somoza dynasty in 1979.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue is an old Sandinista asking whether he would take office in a dictatorship — the charge levelled at Nicaragua's president since his return.

entries.clue: Aversion to heights is never good where always at the summit? (5)

indicatorNotes.where always at the summit?: Always at the summit means the top of every word in turn, and the top of a word written down the grid is the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: the opening letter of each of those five words in order

annotation.surface: Being scared of heights is no use to someone who is always at the top.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Aversion' leans on the idiom: to have a thing about heights is to dread them. Nothing says 'initial', so 'at the summit' has to do that work in a down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: Aversion → THING: having a thing about something is the idiom for a hang-up about it, a dread you cannot quite account for.

entries.clue: Sky, might you have said? Oddly it’s blue! (4)

indicatorNotes.Oddly: Oddly points at the odd-numbered letters — the first, the third, the fifth and the seventh of what follows.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of those two words, the apostrophe not counting

annotation.surface: Remarking on the oddly blue colour of the sky.
annotation.walkthrough: Skye, in the Inner Hebrides off Scotland's west coast, is spelt with a final E that the clue quietly drops — which is what 'might you have said' licenses.
annotation.definitionFit: Sky, might you have said? → ISLE: heard aloud that is Skye, one of the Hebrides, so the answer is what Skye is rather than a synonym for it.

entries.clue: Particular Turner turned up? (4)

indicatorNotes.turned up: Turned up in a down clue means read the letters from the bottom of the column to the top.

blocks.note: Lana Turner was a Hollywood star of the 1940s, and her first name is what gets turned

annotation.surface: A particular Turner painting coming to light.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Turner' is the film star and not the painter the surface offers — Lana Turner, of The Postman Always Rings Twice.
annotation.definitionFit: Particular → ANAL: anal is the clipped form of anally retentive, the word for someone fussy over tiny details.

entries.clue: Member of the orchestra I understand, violin player picked up? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: A member of the orchestra is usually one of the players, but the instruments are equally the orchestra's constituents — the oboes, the horns, the strings — and that is the sense wanted here.

indicatorNotes.picked up: Picked up means caught by ear, so what matters is how the words sound rather than how they are spelt.

blocks.note: oh is the cry of someone who has just seen the point, and it needs only its first letter written down
the bow is what plays a violin, and heard rather than read it is spelt out to the end of the answer

annotation.surface: Agreeing about a violinist heard playing somewhere nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Violin player' is the bow rather than the person holding it, which is where the clue turns. Picked up does double duty: you pick a bow up, and you pick a sound up.
annotation.definitionFit: Member of the orchestra → OBOE: the oboe is the double-reed woodwind whose A the whole orchestra tunes to before a concert.

entries.clue: Queasy one, relative gulping oxygen is in a state (10)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer rather than replacing it: the answer names a person, and what the clue says of them is that they live in a state.

indicatorNotes.gulping: To gulp a thing down is to take it inside, so what follows is swallowed whole by the word before.

blocks.note: feeling queasy is feeling ill
I is one in Roman numerals
nan is what British children call their grandmother
O is oxygen's symbol on the periodic table
the word itself, swallowed along with the oxygen

annotation.surface: A queasy patient and a relative gulping oxygen, everyone in a panic.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In a state' is a flap on the surface and a US state underneath, Illinois. The little word 'is' gets swallowed too, which is the easiest piece to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: in a state → ILLINOISAN: an Illinoisan lives in Illinois, so the answer is somebody in a state rather than a word for the state itself.

entries.clue: Spot channel on the radio? (4)

indicatorNotes.on the radio: Heard on the radio and never seen, so the word is wanted for its sound and not its spelling.

blocks.note: a moat is the water channel dug round a castle wall

annotation.surface: Picking out a station on the radio dial.
annotation.walkthrough: A mote is a speck of dust, the word the Bible uses for the mote in your brother's eye. 'Channel' is the water round a castle, not a station.
annotation.definitionFit: Spot → MOTE: a mote is a tiny speck drifting in a sunbeam, about the smallest spot there is.

entries.clue: Victorian author set to field question left after fumbles overheard? (3,7)

indicatorNotes.to field: To field a question is to take it and deal with it, so the question named next is caught inside.
indicatorNotes.after: After puts everything built so far later in the answer than the piece named beyond it.
indicatorNotes.overheard: Overheard means caught by ear, so the word is wanted for its sound rather than its spelling.

blocks.note: to fumble a catch is to miss it, and misses said aloud is how the title is spoken
jelly sets by gelling, so to set is to gel
to question someone is to ask them
L is the standard short form of left

annotation.surface: A cricketer taking questions in the field after dropping a catch.
annotation.walkthrough: Elizabeth Gaskell wrote Cranford and North and South and was published as Mrs Gaskell all her working life. The cricket picture rests on 'field' and 'fumbles', neither of which is doing its surface job.
annotation.definitionFit: Victorian author → MRS GASKELL: Elizabeth Gaskell, novelist of Cranford and North and South, published under her married title throughout Victoria's reign.
